title: The Assistant Must Not Become the Store
description: I am connecting an assistant to the catalog, not replacing the catalog. The assistant can ask the tools that already exist.
body:
An assistant that keeps the files in the chat has already chosen the wrong store. The conversation ends. The permissions never made the trip. What you have left is a plausible summary with no record to inspect.

Today I connect an assistant to VALESKA through the Model Context Protocol so it can ask the index that already exists. The five tools from the November 29 milestone remain the surface: search, classify, scan, list categories, retrieve file information. The new work is a client, two playbooks, and the start of a recovery agent. It is not a second memory.

The wrong default

The usual move is to pour a repository into a model and hope the model remembers. That is convenient for a demonstration. It is fatal as an architecture. The files, the APQC classifications, and the embeddings have to live where they can be reviewed tomorrow by someone who was not in the conversation.

A librarian does not become the library because she can walk the stacks. She uses a catalog that remains when she leaves. The assistant should be able to request a scan, ask a question in ordinary language, and read what the tools return. It should not replace those returns with an opaque history.

A client, not a cabinet

The client library speaks to the MCP server already running. It maps assistant requests onto those five tools and carries context between the two. The code is written so a provider can be swapped: an abstract interface, a Claude implementation, a runner that executes a playbook. That is an interface, not a claim that several vendors are in daily use. The tests construct the client with a fake key. They do not prove a live model call.

Two playbooks turn tool access into a method another person can repeat. Codebase onboarding scans a directory and asks what languages, components, and shape the project has. Feature investigation turns a natural-language question into semantic search and returns material about a function. They are sequences: establish the scope, gather evidence, interpret the return, propose a next look. They are prompt-shaped methods on top of the tools. They are not a recorded run against a stranger’s tree.

Proposal is not permission

The same commit lays a chaos-recovery agent. The intent is clear enough: notice deep nesting, mixed types, and poor names; draft an organization plan; estimate risk; let a person confirm before anything moves. The execution path is supposed to include safety checks and a dry run. The file is a foundation. Several of its scores are still placeholders. A system that can see disorder should be able to explain the evidence and propose a sequence. It should not confuse that proposal with authority to rearrange the project.

What the four tests show

Phase 3 reports four passing tests: client initialization, tool communication, playbook execution, and end-to-end integration. Read them as construction tests. They do not stand in for a live MCP session or a live assistant. The architectural result is still real: an assistant can be pointed at a governed tool surface instead of being asked to become the filing cabinet.

The next work is to run those playbooks against a codebase we did not write, and to make recovery something a person can confirm rather than a skeleton. Until then this is a client we can execute, not a claim that the assistant already understands the work.

Historical basis: VALESKA Phase 3 commit 8a5aa55, November 30, 2025; contemporaneous Phase 3 summary, valeska/ai_client.py, valeska/chaos_recovery_agent.py, and test_phase3.py. The Phase 3 summary is internally dated December 2025; the commit timestamp is the publication-date authority.

data.coverAlt: A night library with a drafting table, an open blueprint, and a brass instrument joined by a thread of light to a distant city: the assistant consulting the catalog rather than replacing it.
